extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, regulated employers, industry trade associations, OSHA stakeholders, regulatory economists, and commenters on the HCS rule
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methodological criteria used by OSHA to estimate counts (containers, labels, SDSs), assess technological feasibility, and calculate compliance costs and cost savings for revisions to the Hazard Communication Standard (HCS). Intended to support regulatory economic analysis and public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shipment weight per container formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Shipment Weight = (Product Weight per gallon × Container Capacity) + Container Weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA estimated representative weight per container for various container sizes and substances using representative substances. Where data were lacking on product weight by container type, professional judgment was used to select a "typical" product weight per gallon and container weight. No commenter provided data that contradicted this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of shipment tons/pounds to number of containers
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert CFS data on tons (or pounds) shipped by container size into a number of containers by estimating the percentage of each shipment class likely to be shipped in certain container sizes, multiplying total hazardous pounds by that percentage, then dividing by average weight per container type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shipments of lower weights are generally estimated to be shipped in smaller containers, and vice versa; analysis relies on estimated percentage shipped in each container type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate of number of labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate average number of labels on a single container for each container size and multiply by the number of containers to estimate total labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimates account for outer packaging that would require an additional label (e.g., kits where tags/fold-out labels infeasible) and grouped containers shipped in an outer container with a label. Results reported in Table VI-5 and separate column for very small containers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of very small containers (≤3 ml) for label estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: The same label-estimation analysis is performed limited to containers with volume capacity of 3 ml or less to estimate labels on very small containers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed paragraph (f)(12)(iii) would allow only a product identifier on very small containers (3 ml or less) where the manufacturer/importer/distributor can demonstrate that a label would interfere with normal use and it is not feasible to use pull-out labels, fold-back labels, or tags; immediate outer packaging must include the full label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation from SCTG codes to NAICS industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocate number of labels shipped from SCTG codes to NAICS codes using a NAICS-to-SCTG mapping adapted from the 2012 FEA, with NAICS categories updated to 2017.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use U.S. Census Statistics of U.S. Businesses data to estimate each NAICS industry's share of total receipts for the SCTG code and allocate labels proportionally. Perform calculation separately for shipments from manufacturers and from distributors when estimating impacts of released-for-shipment provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative assumption when data are lacking (FIFRA/pesticide example)
rubrics_metrics.description: When OSHA lacks data indicating the proportion of chemicals exempt (e.g., pesticides under FIFRA), the agency errs on the side of caution and includes labels in estimates, noting that any overstatement will over-estimate costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption does not change the statutory scope; it only affects magnitude of estimated costs and leads to conservative (higher) cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invitation to comment and evidence on methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA invited public comment on the reasonableness of its methodology for estimating SDSs and labels and on understanding of electronic template files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency reviews comments (e.g., Ameren agreed, others raised concerns) and addresses them in the rulemaking record; methodology may be defended or revised based on substantive input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological feasibility legal standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard is technologically feasible if the protective measures it requires already exist, can be brought into existence with available technology, or can be created with technology reasonably expected to be developed (see Lead I, 647 F.2d at 1272).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA must demonstrate this standard when promulgating occupational safety and health standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of technological feasibility for HCS revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA determined that compliance with the final rule is technologically feasible for all affected industries because required changes are mainly revisions to presentation of information (reclassification and SDS/label revisions) and do not require new technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency reviewed comments about software capability and concluded existing software and practices (narrative fields, external SDS vendors) indicate feasibility; lack of tailored software does not make a requirement infeasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for demonstrating technological infeasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A commenter asserting technological infeasibility must show that technological barriers prevent development of compliant solutions; mere statements that current software lacks features are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA cites sample SDSs showing narrative content is routinely provided and notes that even if some programs lack features, that does not make compliance infeasible (cite Lead I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Released-for-shipment provision effect on labeling practicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Revised released-for-shipment provisions will alleviate concerns about practicability (e.g., breaking down pallets of sealed/shrink-wrapped packages to replace labels) and reduce the risk of injury associated with re-labeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both a feasibility and a cost-savings consideration; OSHA solicited comments and received none challenging feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five main cost and cost-savings categories to include in FEA
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated costs and cost savings consist of: (1) cost of revising SDSs and labels for reclassifications and language criteria; (2) management familiarization and related management costs; (3) employee training costs; (4) cost savings from released-for-shipment provision; and (5) cost savings from limiting labeling for certain very small containers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First three categories considered one-time costs; last two categories are annual cost savings. OSHA requested comment on whether any other elements would cause costs or savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of prior compliance costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated costs and cost savings are based on employers achieving full compliance with new requirements and do not include prior costs and cost savings associated with firms already in compliance with the revised requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA estimates incremental costs only — activities newly conducted to conform to the revisions. Does not estimate costs already required under the 2012 HCS that remain in place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annualization and discounting methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: All costs and cost savings are expressed in annualized terms for comparison; a 7-percent discount rate was applied to calculate present values and to annualize over a 10-year period. Economic effects using a 3-percent rate are provided in supporting spreadsheets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annualized costs represent the appropriate measure for assessing longer-term impacts and comparing net costs across regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of overhead and loaded wage calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: To calculate loaded labor cost, OSHA adds base wage + fringe benefits (45% of base wage) + overhead (17% of base wage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overhead rate of 17% adopted as consistent with prior FEAs; example loaded wages given for Manager, Logistics Personnel, Production Worker, and Occupational Health and Safety Specialist with specific SOC codes and dollar amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and case-specific treatment of overhead costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Overhead costs are indirect expenses (rent, utilities, office equipment) with no general consensus on elements; treatment must be case-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA adopted 17% for this FEA and justifies consistency with prior analyses (2017 Form 300A delay FEA, 2016 silica FEA). Lack of consensus explained as reason for case-specific choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline compliance assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: With the exception of provisions addressing precautionary statements and other mandatory language, OSHA estimated baseline compliance of zero percent for the revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baseline compliance for Appendices C and D (precautionary statements etc.) is discussed separately; where baseline compliance nonzero, it is reflected in cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture of compliance resource use irrespective of procurement mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated compliance costs are intended to capture resources required for compliance regardless of whether establishments use internal labor or purchase services/products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where outsourcing occurs (e.g., SDS software vendors, contracted SDS creation), costs are still counted because they represent resources expended to achieve compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of indirect market impacts absent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The FEA does not include indirect costs or impacts that may result from reclassification or relabeling (e.g., changes in production or product demand) because OSHA received no input on such changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with the 2012 determination; theoretical indirect impacts acknowledged but not assessed without stakeholder input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption on timing of compliance costs (first-year assumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: For annualizing costs, OSHA assumed all compliance costs will be incurred in the first year, notwithstanding phased compliance dates; this simplifying assumption may upwardly bias cost estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA recognizes phased implementation of 18, 24, 36, and 42 months for different provisions but used immediate implementation for conservative estimation and to support economic feasibility determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of phased updates within normal document revision cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA expects many firms will phase in SDS and label revisions according to normal cycles (product introductions, reformulations, marketing changes) and therefore may not need to replace existing labels or SDSs immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency extended phase-in periods in final rule (per paragraph j) to facilitate firms making revisions in one round and to reduce costs; some firms already aligning with GHS internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior FEAs and contractor analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated costs draw partly on analysis from the 2012 HCS final rule FEA and partly on new analysis by OSHA's contractor ERG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologies and assumptions from prior FEAs (e.g., approach to estimating affected SDS templates) inform current estimates but are adapted where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-specific affected template factor (50% rule for certain NAICS)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the PEA OSHA estimated that approximately 50 percent of the SDS electronic templates in identified NAICS industries (aerosols, desensitized explosives, flammable gases) would be affected by the proposed reclassification requirements; this factor was applied to derive number of directly affected electronic files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 50% factor is an analytic assumption used to estimate affected electronic files and can be challenged or supported by commenters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sources and updating approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Census CFS, U.S. Census SUSB, IRS SOI Tax Stats, BEA GDP deflator, and updated NAICS mappings (2007→2017) to estimate shipments, receipts, revenues, and profit rates for affected industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA extrapolated 2017 SUSB receipts to 2022 dollars using BEA GDP deflator and benchmarked per-establishment revenue to payroll per 2017 revenue-payroll ratios. Profit rates based on IRS SOI Corporation Source Book (2000–2013).
